title: Kaifeng
hookLine: a Jewish community in China, in the city of Kaifeng on the Yellow River

cards: A Jesuit priest named Matteo Ricci is living in Beijing when a visitor arrives. The man has heard there are foreigners in the city who worship one God and are not Muslims, and he has come to meet fellow believers.
He is from Kaifeng. As they talk, it slowly becomes clear that the visitor is not a Christian at all. He is a Jew, from a community that has lived in China for generations.
Neither man had expected the other.

teach.b: Kaifeng was once an imperial capital on the Yellow River. Jewish merchants came there, tradition says, along the trade routes from Persia, and stayed.
They built a synagogue in a courtyard, Chinese in its architecture, with Torah scrolls inside.
They put up stone steles, carved in Chinese, telling their history and their faith in words their neighbors could read.

teach.h: THE RELIGION THAT PLUCKS THE SINEW.
teach.b: Their neighbors had their own name for them: the religion that plucks out the sinew. That name points straight back to Genesis.
After Jacob wrestles through the night and his thigh is touched, the Torah says: "Therefore the children of Israel eat not the sinew of the thigh-vein." The Jews of Kaifeng kept that rule.
They removed the sinew from their meat, and the people around them noticed. A practice from a story about Jacob became the name their neighbors called them by. The community had a hard road.
The Yellow River flooded, and the synagogue was damaged more than once and rebuilt. Over time, with no new teachers arriving and no rabbis to train, Hebrew faded and the community thinned.
The synagogue was eventually gone. Yet some families in Kaifeng still remember that their ancestors were Jews, and some have reconnected with Jewish life.
Some of the scrolls and steles survived and are kept in museums and libraries.

teach.h: A RULE FROM GENESIS, KEPT IN CHINA.
teach.b: Kaifeng shows how far a single rule from Genesis could travel, and how long it could be kept.

how: Descendants of Kaifeng's Jews remember their heritage in family memory, and some study Hebrew and Jewish practice today; scholars study the surviving steles and scrolls.

games.q: you are a visitor from Kaifeng in Beijing. you hear foreigners there worship one God and are not Muslims. what do you think?
games.why: he thought Ricci was a fellow believer; only as they talked did it become clear he was a Jew and Ricci a Christian.

practice: Bring back the one picture from today that stays with you: the visitor in Beijing, the stone steles, or the name the neighbors gave. Then think of a small habit of your own that people know you by, and who passed it to you.

wordCard.voice: Kaifeng. The city on the Yellow River where a Jewish community built a synagogue, carved its story in Chinese on stone, and kept the sinew rule from Genesis. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: china. A rule from Genesis, kept a long way from home. See you next time.
